name: Ivar Kreuger

summary.text: Ivar Kreuger was a Swedish industrialist who built a group of match companies and holding companies (Kreuger & Toll, Swedish Match, International Match Corporation) that raised large sums from American investors through the Boston investment bank Lee, Higginson & Co. He died in Paris in March 1932. Price Waterhouse & Co., called in by the Swedish government, reported within weeks that the 1930 balance sheet of Kreuger & Toll misrepresented the company's position, and Swedish authorities reported finding forged Italian treasury bills among his papers.

sources.title: The Kreuger Affair: It is no longer possible to doubt

facts.claim: Price Waterhouse & Co. began auditing the Kreuger books eleven days after Kreuger's death in Paris in March 1932 and within a month concluded that he had falsified them.
facts.quote: Eleven days after a pistol shot in Paris put an end to Ivar Kreuger's fantastic dreams of a match empire, Price, Waterhouse & Co. sat down to audit the Kreuger books. Within a month they pronounced Ivar Kreuger a crook.

facts.claim: Price Waterhouse's April 1932 report concluded that the 1930 balance sheet of Kreuger & Toll misrepresented the true financial position of the company.
facts.quote: The April 1932 report concluded that its 1930 Balance Sheet: 'misrepresented the true financial position of the company'.

facts.claim: Price Waterhouse traced Kreuger's manipulations back to 1917 through the ledgers of about a dozen holding companies and 140 operating subsidiaries and trading concerns, and estimated that Kreuger had diverted about $115 million.
facts.quote: Threading their way through the ledgers of a dozen holding companies, 140 operating subsidiaries and trading concerns, Price, Waterhouse traced his manipulations back to 1917.

facts.claim: In April 1932 The Spectator reported that Swedish authorities had found among Kreuger's papers forged Italian Treasury bills, carried as assets in the books of Kreuger & Toll, and a forged contract for a Spanish loan of 180 million pesetas.
facts.quote: The Swedish authorities have found among his papers a forged contract for a Spanish loan of 180,000,000 pesetas, and forged Italian Treasury bills

sources.title: The Kreuger Affair: It is no longer possible to doubt

facts.claim: A reference-work biography states that after a proposed Italian match-monopoly deal fell through, Kreuger counterfeited forty-two Italian bonds, each with a face value of 500,000 pounds, bearing a forged signature of the Italian finance minister.
facts.quote: he counterfeited forty-two Italian bonds, each with a face value of £500,000 and a forged signature of the Italian finance minister

facts.claim: Lee, Higginson & Co., Kreuger's American banking house, accepted audits by Swedish firms rather than requiring a United States audit of Kreuger's companies.
facts.quote: It was persuaded by Ivar Kreuger... that it was not necessary for a U. S. firm to audit his vast affairs. He had not only one but three great Swedish firms of auditors... So great was Sweden's reputation for honesty that Lee, Higginson decided, as a practical matter, to accept a Swedish audit of the greatest Swede.

connections.claim: Lee, Higginson & Co. of Boston acted as Kreuger's American banking house and accepted Swedish audits of his companies instead of commissioning a United States audit.
connections.quote: So great was Sweden's reputation for honesty that Lee, Higginson decided, as a practical matter, to accept a Swedish audit of the greatest Swede.

connections.claim: Price Waterhouse & Co. audited the Kreuger companies after Kreuger's death in 1932 and reported that the books had been falsified.
connections.quote: Within a month they pronounced Ivar Kreuger a crook.

openQuestions: The site says Kreuger forged 42 Italian treasury bills with a face value of about 28.7 million pounds (about $142 million). Sources differ: EBSCO gives 42 bills of 500,000 pounds each (21 million pounds); The Spectator's 1932 report gives a figure of about 21 million; a popular site gives 500 million lire (about $142 million). The count and value need a scholarly biography or the 1932 Swedish inquiry record.

The site's figure of 'some 400 subsidiaries' was not confirmed. Time's 1932 account of the Price Waterhouse audit refers to a dozen holding companies and 140 operating subsidiaries and trading concerns; one popular source refers to 400 companies.
The site's claim that auditors found 'at least $250 million' of reported assets missing or fictitious was not confirmed; Time reported Price Waterhouse's figure of $115 million.
The claim that Lee, Higginson & Co. was dissolved in 1932 and reorganized as Lee Higginson Corporation, and the role of partner Donald Durant, were not found in the sources returned.
Two Time archive pieces ('Kreuger's Books' and 'Greatest Crook') were returned together; the owner should check which of the two carries each quoted passage.
The Accounting History Review quote on the April 1932 report is attributed on the basis of the search summary; confirm against the article abstract or full text.
